title: Is jazz ever dead; disc jockeys and jazz teaching in schools
summary: Sam says jazz has never died, blames uninformed disc jockeys, and welcomes jazz musicians teaching in schools.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That's, that--you lead right into the other half of the question I wanted to ask you about something you said before like the common cliche that jazz being dead and suddenly it's been reborn again. Is Jazz ever dead?
No. Jazz is never been dead, man.
Because they don't know any better, man. You know?
It's more or less the exposure they've had--

Exactly, that's what it is, you know. And then you got, the, the, like I say, you got disc jockeys on the air, man, push--they don't know any better. If they know, if...there are disc jockeys that that knew better, they aren't there any more. They was fired, or either they quit. So disc jockeys they know nothing. Now on the air now, they don't know any better, man.
And the young people rule the world--

And it's also, also the young people, they don't know it either because they have no one to tell them to to to show them, to teach them. That's why, it's uh, it's uh that's why I'm so happy to see, now, in in in the schools across the country they have jazz musicians in them. To teach people, to teach the students and tell them the truth, man, because the teachers that they have there was, you know, band master, he not going to do anthing but teach you marches, man. And put your butt out there in the field out there and make you

march, and you know, do your routine and marching and stuff, you know. That's all they're going teach you, man. You know. So, so it's I'm so happy to see that, like uh, you and the staff down there at the school--I'll bet you, man that, that kids that come out of school now, are better musicians than they ever was because now they they scope of mind is wide open and they understand, they know, and I see more of the young people in the audience down there than I've ever seen in quite awhile, you know.
/Mr. Ridley is Chairman of the Music department, Livingston College, Rutgers University.

Well, it's been a slow process cause you had a few knuckleheads that come in because--who don't want to hear it. But, you know, there are, more and more like you say that more young people that are really listening and absorbing and realizing, hey this is something I hadn't been exposed to and this history. Because it always has been his story and now we try and tell him our story, as well as, you know.
